words.d: heads-up display: anything on screen that gives the player information, like health or score
the aiming mark (crosshair) that shows where you'll hit
quick-time event: a sudden prompt to press a button in time, or fail
the part of a phone screen that notches, rounded corners and system bars never cover
the parts of the screen a thumb can reach comfortably while holding the phone
a small badge that says "something here needs your attention"
translating and adapting a game for other languages and countries

lessons.title: The HUD: the game's sign language

cards.text: The **HUD** is named after the display projected onto fighter-jet windows. Rogers' definition is broad: **anything visual that gives the player information is HUD.**

The seven classic HUD elements:
- health and targeting
- ammo and inventory
- score
- radar or map
- a context prompt ("press A to open")
The rule for all of them: **clear, clean, simple.**
In mobile F2P, the HUD goes far beyond the play screen. The home screen counts too: currency bars, event buttons, red dots and timers.
Before you add any HUD element, ask: what does the player need to know right now, and what can wait? Everything else is clutter.
The HUD talks without words. If players need subtitles for it, it isn't fluent yet.

check.q: By Rogers' definition, is a mobile home screen with currency bars part of the HUD?
options: Yes: any visual element giving information is HUD
No: only in-game health bars count
Only if it's animated
check.why: Rogers defines HUD as anything visual that informs the player.

lessons.title: Health bars come in many shapes

cards.text: A **health bar** shows how close the player is to losing. It's the most flexible HUD element: a bar, hearts, an orb, a shield or even a heartbeat sound.

Health that slowly comes back, if you wait, keeps players in the game. A game-over screen pulls them out. If you show low health with screen effects, never cover the action. Near death is when players most need to see.
In mobile action games, health sits above each character, where your eyes already are. Brawl Stars does this. In match-3, the **moves left** counter is the level's health bar.

"Lives" that refill on a timer are health stretched over real hours. They pace sessions and earn money. The fail screen ("Out of moves! Continue?") is a business moment: keep it fast, honest and skippable.

check.q: In a match-3 level, what works like a health bar?
options: The moves-left counter
The score
The level number
check.why: Running out of moves ends the level, just like running out of health.

lessons.title: Aiming and gauges on a touchscreen

cards.text: Thumbs aren't precise, so on mobile **aim assist isn't optional.** And the scarcer a resource is, **the bigger and closer its gauge should be.**

Common touch patterns:
- tap attack to auto-target the nearest enemy
- drag to aim manually, and show the range on the ground
- show the aim preview away from the finger, not under it
- give crosshairs a dark outline, so they're visible in sunlight
Clash Royale's elixir bar sits right under your cards, in your thumb's line of sight, because you check it every second. Puzzle games show a small number on each booster icon.
If your design makes a resource scarce, like energy or boosters, its display must be crystal clear. Hiding a scarce resource feels like a trick.
A gauge is a fuel gauge in the desert: the scarcer the fuel, the bigger the gauge.

check.q: Where should a drag-to-aim preview appear?
options: Away from the finger, so it isn't covered
Directly under the thumb, where it's aimed
Only after the shot, to show the result
check.why: The thumb covers part of the screen, so previews must stay visible.

lessons.title: Inventory: never lose the player's stuff

cards.text: An **inventory** lets players see and use what they've collected. Rules: fast access, a nice place to admire loot, readable items, room to grow, and **never lose the player's stuff.**

Items players use often, like boosters, belong in a tray near the thumb, not inside a menu. Use clear shapes and colour-coded rarity frames (grey, green, blue, purple, orange) so items are readable at small sizes.
In merge games like Merge Mansion, the board itself is the inventory. Every slot matters, which makes it a puzzle.

If the inventory is full, send extra items to a mailbox, never delete them. Bought items must never disappear silently. Bigger bags and more slots are a common thing to sell, but limits should feel fair, not like a trap.

check.q: A player's inventory is full when they win a reward. What should happen?
options: Send it to a mailbox so it isn't lost
Delete the new reward to keep things tidy
Delete the player's oldest item instead
check.why: Losing a player's items breaks trust. Store the overflow safely.

cards.text: Games make players feel clumsy in a hundred ways, but rarely make them feel brilliant. **When the player scores, make it BIG and FLASHY.** You can't overdo congratulating the player.

Ways to make rewards feel rewarding:
- a voice or sound that cheers
- coins that fly from where you earned them into the counter
- a short freeze to enjoy the moment
- stars stamping down one by one
Candy Crush's deep voice saying "Sweet!" and "Delicious!" is this rule at huge scale. This polish is often called **juice**.
Two caveats. Routine rewards (your 400th chest) need tap-to-skip or batch opening. And many players play muted, so every celebration must also work visually and with vibration.
For every reward, ask: where are my back-flipping bunnies?

check.q: Why should coins fly into the currency counter?
options: It shows players where their money lives
It slows the game down for drama
It hides the score during rewards
check.why: Cause and effect: the animation teaches where rewards go.

cards.text: A good map answers three questions at a glance: **Where am I? Which way am I facing? Where's the good stuff?** A **context prompt** appears exactly when the player is near something they can use.
Maps need a legend, a theme that fits the game, and must work while you move. On phones, keep the mini-map in a top corner. The bottom corners belong to the thumbs.
In Grand Theft Auto 3, a button icon appears when you stand next to a car you can take. On touch, the prompt is the button: an action button pops up near your thumb.
"Can't do it" feedback matters: a greyed button with a lock or "Level 12" beats a tap that does nothing, which players read as a bug. Show the tutorial hand at first, then fade it out.

check.q: Where should a mobile mini-map usually go?
options: A top corner, away from the thumbs
Bottom centre, where eyes rest
Under the joystick, close to the hand
check.why: Thumbs cover the bottom corners, so information goes up top.

cards.text: Games want to look like movies but still need to inform. Two strategies: **fade the HUD when it isn't needed**, or **remove it and let the world itself communicate.**

A fading HUD must come back when it matters, like when you take damage, and the player needs an easy way to call it back. Without a HUD, use sound, animation, light and effects to show what's important.

The King Kong game (2005) showed a few prompts at the start, then told the player nearly everything through sound and animation. Picture two planets: "No Interface" and "Lots of Interface". Know which one your game lives on.

Hyper-casual games live on Planet No Interface: just a score and a pause button. Mid-core games live on Planet Lots of Interface. Fade what you can: hide the joystick until the thumb lands, collapse event buttons during battle.

check.q: What must a fading HUD do?
options: Return when relevant, easy to call back
Disappear for good once it fades
Fade in over the action when hit
check.why: Hiding the HUD is fine only if players never lose information they need.

lessons.title: Icon design: keep your symbols simple

cards.text: Every icon must be **instantly readable.** Rogers' master rule: **KYSS, Keep Your Symbols Simple.**

- Pick the right image: if it builds tanks, show a tank.
- Use current images. Young testers didn't recognise a postage stamp icon.
- Code with colour, and also with shape.
- No text inside icons: it must be translated and is often too small.

More rules:
- one idea per icon, no mixes of text, character and logo
- a strong dark or light outline so it pops
- view all icons together to catch look-alikes
- don't leave icons to programmers
About 1 in 12 men has some colour blindness, usually red-green. So rarity, team and element colours must also differ by shape or pattern. Review icons at real size on the smallest phone you support.
KYSS: Keep Your Symbols Simple.

check.q: Why use shape as well as colour in icons?
options: Colour-blind players may miss colour differences
Shapes are cheaper for artists to draw
App stores don't allow colour-only icons
check.why: About 1 in 12 men has colour-vision deficiency, so colour alone fails.

lessons.title: Icons and buttons on a phone

cards.text: On phones, icons matter more than anywhere else. **The most important button should be the biggest thing on screen**, and every button needs a generous touch area.
Apple suggests touch targets of about 44 by 44 points. Make the tappable area bigger than the drawn icon. There's no hover on touch, so use long-press or a small "i" button for details.
Brawl Stars has a giant PLAY button. Monopoly GO! has a huge GO button. Coin Master's spin button dominates the screen. The core action is the biggest thing you see.
Your **app icon** is your most important icon: it decides whether people tap in the store. One clear subject, no text, a strong silhouette. Test it at tiny size next to competitors' icons.

check.q: Which button should be the biggest on a mobile home screen?
options: The main play button
The settings button
The news feed panel
check.why: The core action should be the easiest thing to find and tap.

cards.text: A **quick-time event (QTE)** suddenly asks you to press a button in time, or suffer. Players love them or hate them. **Use them only for big cinematic moments.**

Rules for fair QTEs:
- a moment to see the prompt, then a moment to press
- predictable and short
- the same buttons each time
- optional where possible
Pokémon GO's shrinking circle is a timing prompt: throw when the circle is small for a better catch. Success adds a bonus. Failure just means a normal throw.
Prefer "bonus for success" over "death for failure". A required QTE that costs a life feels like a cash grab. Cheap phones and Bluetooth lag make tight timing unfair, so keep windows generous.
A beat to see, a beat to press: ba-DUM.

check.q: Which QTE design is better for F2P?
options: Success gives a bonus; failure just continues
Failure costs the player a life
The timing is random every time
check.why: Optional bonuses reward skill without punishing players unfairly.

lessons.title: Where to put things on screen

cards.text: **Keep the center of the screen for the action.** Put the most important information top-left. Don't fill all the edges.

- Readers' eyes move left to right, so top-left is seen first.
- Full-screen menus can be see-through, so the player stays connected to the world.
- HUD on the left, right and bottom edges makes the view feel tiny. Rogers calls this "bracketing".
Rogers has seen strategy games so packed with panels that playing felt like looking through a mail slot.

On phones:
- keep all buttons inside the **safe area**, away from notches and rounded corners
- put frequent actions in the **thumb zone**
- never put key information where the thumbs rest
- bracketing is the number one disease of F2P home screens

options: HUD on many edges, so the view feels small
A tournament format with brackets
Putting all of the HUD top-left
check.why: Filling the edges shrinks the visible world into a mail slot.

lessons.title: The Three-Press Rule and the first screens

cards.text: Rogers' very important rule: **no screen in the game may ever be more than three presses away.** Players want the good stuff, not a maze of menus.
The title screen is the first thing players see, so it should set the mood. Then get out of the way. Many title-menu options can also live in the pause menu.
On mobile, your real title screen is the **app store page**: icon, screenshots and video. They decide whether people install.

Every screen at launch costs players: system splash, logos, legal text, downloads. Combine and shorten them. New players should be playing within seconds. A frozen-looking loading image reads as a crashed app, so add motion.

check.q: What does the Three-Press Rule say?
options: No screen should be more than three presses away
Every button needs three colours
Show three ads per session
check.why: Deep menus hide features and frustrate players.

cards.text: **Plan the pause screen as carefully as a level.** It's a hub for saving, options, map and inventory. Players should never feel they miss part of the game by pausing.

Saving is one of the most important parts of a game. **Automate it whenever you can.** Offer several save slots, show playtime and chapter names, and never let reloading become a cheap trick to avoid dying.
If you must have loading screens, make them useful: tips, art, a little game. Always show a progress bar, so players know how long to wait.
On mobile, saving is automatic and in the cloud, so players can switch phones without losing progress. The settings, mailbox and profile replace much of the classic pause menu.

check.q: What should every loading screen show?
options: A progress bar or percentage
Nothing but the game logo
A short ad and nothing else
check.why: Players need to know the game hasn't frozen and how long to wait.

cards.text: Fonts follow the same rules as icons: **legible and clear first, themed second.** Avoid overly fancy fonts that are hard to read.

- Strong contrast: never red text on black.
- Text over busy art needs an outline or shadow.
- Size by real size on the smallest phone, held at arm's length.
- Respect the player's system text-size setting.
Supercell's games use chunky fonts with dark outlines. They stay readable over any background, which is why so many mobile games copy the style.
Plan for translation from day one. German words are long, Arabic reads right to left, and Chinese needs different fonts. Never bake text into images: it makes translation and A/B tests painful.
A fancy medieval font on a small phone is a love letter in invisible ink.

check.q: Why give text a dark outline in mobile games?
options: It stays readable over busy, colourful art
App stores require outlines on all text
It makes the text take up less space
check.why: Outlines separate text from any background behind it.

lessons.title: The mobile home screen and red dots

cards.text: Every rule in this level applies to the mobile **home screen (lobby).** **The biggest button is PLAY**, important info sits in the corners, and every feature is one tap from home.
Common layout: profile and level top-left, currencies top-right, each currency with a "+" that opens the right shop section. Group events in one hub button instead of six separate icons.

**Red dots** rules:
- only for things the player can act on
- tapping must clear the dot
- a dot on a sub-tab shows on its parent too
- keep them few, or they all lose meaning
Never fake a red dot to drive players to the shop. It's a dark pattern, and players learn to ignore all your dots.

check.q: A red dot never goes away, even after tapping. What's the problem?
options: Players learn to ignore all dots
Nothing, it looks busy
It increases sales
check.why: Dots must clear when handled, or they stop working as signals.
